chapters.name: Chapter 1: Setting up to work remotely

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Your home workspace and tech basics
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Set up a workspace and check that your tech is ready for remote work.
This lesson builds toward: At home or in the place you plan to work, you will set up a workspace and check your internet, headset and account security, with a speed test done, two-step sign-in on and a screen lock set.
You need a reliable internet connection, a computer (many jobs do not allow phone-only work), a headset or earbuds with a microphone, and a quiet spot. A small table by a wall works. Good light in front of you, not behind, helps on camera.
Check your internet with a free speed test before applying. If it is slow or you do not have home internet, ask your library, workforce program or internet provider about low-cost options; some programs change, so check what is available where you live.
Protect work accounts like your own: strong passphrases, two-step sign-in, software updates, and no work on public computers unless your employer allows it. Lock your screen when you step away.
Step by step:
- Choose a quiet spot with a table and good light in front of you.
- Get a headset or earbuds with a microphone.
- Run a free internet speed test.
- Turn on updates, two-step sign-in and a screen lock.
- Ask about low-cost internet if you need it.
Words to know:
- Remote work: doing your job from home or another place outside the employer's office.
- Headset: headphones with a microphone.
- Bandwidth: how much data your internet can carry; more is better for video.
Try it now: Set up your workspace, run an internet speed test, and write a checklist of what you have and what you still need.
You can now set up a safe, workable home workspace.

check.q: Which item do many remote jobs require besides internet?
check.why: Many remote jobs do not allow phone-only work, so you need a computer.

check.q: Your speed test shows slow internet and you want to apply for remote jobs. What do you do?
options: Ask your library, workforce program or internet provider about low-cost options
Apply anyway and hope it works
Use a stranger's Wi-Fi without asking
check.why: Libraries, workforce programs and providers may know about low-cost internet options.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Joining and running video calls
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Join a video call professionally and handle common problems.
This lesson builds toward: Given a meeting link, you will join a video call and use mute, camera, chat and screen sharing, joining early and fixing a sound problem without help.
Most remote jobs use video tools like Zoom, Microsoft Teams or Google Meet. You usually join by clicking a link in an email or calendar invite. Join two or three minutes early to fix any problems.
Know the basic controls: mute and unmute, turn the camera on and off, share your screen, and use the chat. Stay muted when you are not talking. Look at the camera when you speak, and use your name as your display name.
If something breaks: check that the right microphone and speaker are selected in settings, leave and rejoin, or call in by phone if the invite has a number. Tell the host in the chat. Many tools also offer live captions and AI-made meeting summaries; follow your employer's rules about using them.
Step by step:
- Click the meeting link two or three minutes early.
- Check your display name, camera and microphone.
- Stay muted when not speaking.
- Use the chat to say if you have problems.
- If audio fails, check device settings or rejoin.
Words to know:
- Mute: turn off your microphone so others cannot hear you.
- Screen share: show your computer screen to others on the call.
- Captions: words on screen showing what people say.
Try it now: Start a free test meeting with a friend, family member or yourself in Zoom, Teams or Google Meet. Practice mute, camera, chat and screen share.
You can now join and take part in a video call professionally and fix common problems.

check.q: What does screen sharing do on a video call?
options: Shows your computer screen to others on the call
check.why: Screen sharing shows your screen to the other people on the call.

check.q: Your audio stops working in a team meeting. What do you do?
options: Tell the host in the chat, check your device settings or rejoin
check.why: Use the chat to tell the host, then check settings, rejoin or call in by phone.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Writing clear work messages with AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write short, clear, professional work messages with AI help.
This lesson builds toward: Given a work situation, you will write a short, clear work message with AI help, leading with the point, saying what you need and by when, with no customer data in unapproved AI tools.
In remote work, most communication is written: chat (like Teams or Slack) and email. Clear writing is the top remote skill. Lead with the point, keep it short, and say what you need and by when.
AI can help: "Turn this into a short, polite message to my manager: I finished the 40 customer records, 3 had missing phone numbers, should I call them or skip them?" Then check it sounds like you and is not too formal.
Useful message types: a daily status update (done, doing next, blocked), a clear question, and a heads-up when you are late or sick. Never paste customer data, passwords or company secrets into an AI tool your employer has not approved.
Step by step:
- Start with the main point.
- Say what you need and by when.
- Ask AI to make it short and polite.
- Check it sounds like you.
- Keep customer and company data out of unapproved AI tools.
Words to know:
- Status update: a short message about what you did, what is next and any problems.
- Chat app: a work messaging tool like Microsoft Teams or Slack.
Try it now: With AI help, write three messages: a status update, a question to a manager, and an "I'm running 15 minutes late" note. Edit each to sound like you.
You can now write clear, short work messages with AI help.

check.q: What three things go in a daily status update?
options: Your lunch, your mood and the weather
What you did, what is next and anything blocking you
check.why: A status update says what is done, what is next and what is blocked.

check.q: You want AI to help write a message about a customer complaint. What do you leave out?
options: What you need from your manager
The customer's name and phone number
check.why: Never paste customer data into an AI tool your employer has not approved.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Working well and finding remote jobs

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Working in shared documents
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Edit, comment and suggest changes in a shared document.
This lesson builds toward: Given a shared document link, you will add a comment, make a suggested change and open version history, without changing the sharing settings.
Remote teams work in the same document at once using Google Docs, Google Sheets or Microsoft 365 (Word, Excel) online. You open it from a shared link and can see others' changes as they type.
Learn three moves. Comment: highlight text and add a comment to ask or suggest without changing it. Suggest: Google Docs has Suggesting mode and Word has Track Changes, so your edits show for others to accept. Version history lets you see or restore earlier versions.
Be careful with sharing settings: share only with the people who need it, and do not change "anyone with the link" settings without asking. Many tools have built-in AI (such as Gemini in Google Workspace or Copilot in Microsoft 365) if your employer turns it on.
Step by step:
- Open the shared document from its link.
- Highlight text and add a comment.
- Turn on Suggesting mode (Google Docs) or Track Changes (Word) and make an edit.
- Open version history to see earlier versions.
- Check sharing settings before sharing further.
Words to know:
- Shared document: a file several people can open and edit online.
- Comment: a note attached to part of a document.
- Version history: a record of earlier versions of a file that you can view or restore.
Try it now: Create a Google Doc or Word online document, share it with someone you trust, and practice a comment, a suggested edit and viewing version history together.
You can now collaborate in a shared document with comments, suggestions and version history.

check.q: What does Track Changes do in Word?
options: Shows your edits so others can review and accept them
check.why: Track Changes shows edits for others to accept, like Suggesting mode in Google Docs.

check.q: A teammate asks you to share the team document with a friend outside the company. What do you do?
options: Change it to "anyone with the link"
Check with the document's owner before sharing further
Copy the whole document into an email
check.why: Share only with people who need it, and ask before changing sharing settings.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Managing your own time
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Plan a remote workday with time blocks and clear start and stop times.
This lesson builds toward: Given a list of tasks for a workday, you will create a time-block plan with start, break and stop times, that fits your real life and ends with a status update.
At home, nobody walks by your desk. You manage your own time. Set a regular start time, breaks and a stop time, and tell the people you live with when you are working.
Time-blocking helps: divide the day into blocks for focused work, messages, meetings and breaks. Ask AI: "Make a time-block plan for my workday from 9 to 5 with a 30-minute lunch. Tasks: [list]. Put focused work in the morning and check messages at set times."
Track what you finish. At the end of the day, write a short status update. If you are struggling with distractions, childcare or health, tell your manager early; many have options if they know.
Step by step:
- Set start, break and stop times.
- List today's tasks.
- Ask AI for a time-block plan.
- Adjust it to your real life.
- End the day with a short status update.
Words to know:
- Time-blocking: planning your day in blocks of time for specific tasks.
- Focused work: work done without interruptions.
Try it now: Ask AI for a time-block plan for a real or practice workday, adjust it, and follow it for at least half a day. Write a short end-of-day update.
You can now plan and manage a remote workday with time blocks.

options: A set part of the day for one kind of task
check.why: Time-blocking divides the day into blocks for focused work, messages, meetings and breaks.

check.q: AI's time-block plan puts focused work at 3 pm, when your kids get home from school. What do you do?
options: Move focused work to a quieter time that fits your real life
check.why: Adjust the AI plan to your real life.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Finding real remote jobs and avoiding scams
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Search for remote jobs on trusted sources and spot work-from-home scams.
This lesson builds toward: Given a remote job post, you will check whether the job is real or a work-from-home scam, using every warning sign before sharing any private numbers.
Search trusted places: company career pages, well-known job sites, your state's job bank and your local American Job Center. Use the filter for "remote" and read where the job allows you to live; some remote jobs are only for certain states or countries.
Work-from-home scams are common. The FTC warns about promises of big pay for little work, being asked to pay for starter kits, training or certifications, being sent a check to deposit and send part back, and reshipping packages. Honest employers do not charge you to get a job.
Check before you share: look up the company yourself, make sure the email comes from the company's real domain (not a free email address), and be wary of interviews done only by text chat. Do not give bank or Social Security numbers until you have a verified offer. Report scams at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.
Step by step:
- Search trusted job sources with the remote filter.
- Check where the job allows you to live.
- Look up the company on your own.
- Watch for fees, checks to deposit, reshipping and text-only interviews.
- Share private numbers only after a verified offer.
Words to know:
- Work-from-home scam: a fake remote job meant to steal money or information.
- Domain: the part of an email or web address after the @ or www, like company.com.
Official sources:
- FTC: Job scams
- ReportFraud.ftc.gov
Try it now: Final task: find one real remote job post, check it against the scam signs, and save it. Add it to your workspace checklist, video call test, three messages, shared-document practice and time-block plan to finish your remote work readiness kit.
You can now get set up, communicate, collaborate and manage time for remote work, and find real remote jobs safely.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Workspace and tech No speed test, or two-step sign-in or screen lock is off. A workspace photo or checklist with a speed test, headset, two-step sign-in and screen lock. Light is in front of the learner and a backup plan exists if the internet fails. Video call ready The call test was not done, or mute and camera controls were not found. A one-minute call test or checklist showing display name, mute, camera and chat. Also practiced screen sharing and fixing a sound problem. Work messages Fewer than three messages, or a message buries the point or includes private data. A status update, a question to a manager and a late note, each short and leading with the point. Each says what is needed and by when, and sounds like the learner. Shared document No comment or suggested change in the document. A comment and a suggested change in a shared document. Also opened version history and left the sharing settings unchanged. Time-block plan No start, break or stop times. A one-day plan with start, break and stop times and blocks for tasks. Fits the learner's real life and ends with a status update. Job post checked The job post was not checked for scam signs. One real remote job post checked against the warning signs, with the company looked up. Also notes where the job allows people to live and the email domain used. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Which is a warning sign of a work-from-home scam?
options: The job post lists where you can live
The recruiter emails from the company's own domain
The company has a career page
You must pay for a starter kit before you begin
check.why: Honest employers do not charge you to get a job.

check.q: A "company" offers a remote job after a text-only interview and asks for your bank number now. What do you do?
options: Send it to get paid faster
Do not share it; look up the company yourself and report it if it is a scam
Send your Social Security number instead
Ask them to text you a check
check.why: Text-only interviews and early requests for bank numbers are warning signs; share private numbers only after a verified offer.
